About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Religious Studies Years 11–13 of
the New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Religious Studies Years 11–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Religious Studies Years 11–13 is proposed to
be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Religious Studies Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11
from 1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January
2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Religious Studies, students are taught about religious and spiritual beliefs and
  practices, and how these shape individuals and societies. Students are taught
  how religious and spiritual traditions influence, and are influenced by diverse
  worldviews, ethical decision-making, identity, global perspectives, and the course
  of history.

Students are taught core knowledge about religious and spiritual worldviews and how
beliefs, practices and traditions shape identity, meaning, ethics, and society. Students
know and understand that informed and respectful engagement with religious
diversity is important for understanding people and the world.

Religious Studies provides students with the knowledge and practices to analyse and
apply understandings of beliefs, histories, texts, and ethical systems in real-world and
theoretical contexts, including interpreting religious information. This disciplinary
knowledge helps students to develop expertise in evaluating and synthesising
different perspectives and representing and communicating understanding using
relevant concepts, conventions, and vocabulary.

As students progress through Years 11–13, they are taught to interpret, analyse, and
draw conclusions from increasingly complex religious or spiritual information to make
justified decisions in written form. This enables them to evaluate diverse perspectives
and communicate decisions that are evidence-based and grounded in a broader
understanding of identity, meaning, justice, human dignity, and religious diversity.

  Religious Studies lead to pathways in humanities, law, education, and
  international relations.

 Disciplinary Writing


 Focus: The use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Religious Studies, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to describe, explain, interpret, analyse, evaluate, and justify understandings of religious or spiritual beliefs,
 practices, narratives, histories, and ethical perspectives, using relevant evidence, concepts, and disciplinary vocabulary for specific purposes and audiences.
